newsitem.title: CANADA: DiamondWorks may remove Sierra Leone staff.
newsitem.headline: DiamondWorks may remove Sierra Leone staff.

text.p: DiamondWorks Ltd said Friday it is preparing a contingency plan to evacuate its staff from Sierra Leone if security at its diamond property worsens.
Sierra Leone President Ahmad Tejan was overthrown in a military coup last weekend and the United States on Friday evacuated nearly 1,000 people from Freetown, capital of the African country.

DiamondWorks Chairman Eric Friedland told the company's annual meeting in Vancouver that staff at its mine at Koidu, 250 km west of Freetown, reported on Friday that the situation there remained calm. Relations with the local military were "cordial and non-confrontational," he said.
Friedland declined to specify how many foreign citizens worked for the company at Koidu, citing security concerns.
But he said 35 expatriates including Candians, Americans, Russians along with 100 local Lebanese businessman had also sought shelter there.
"We are preparing a contingency plan to evacuate our employees and these other people. We have a moral obligation to protect these people and we will," he said.
DiamondWorks had already enlisted a private firm of military experts to guard its operations in Sierra Leone.
Work at the site, where DiamondWorks has US$5 million in equipment, stopped about 10 days ago.

But the military coup has so far not delayed its work significantly, Friedland said. The company was focusing on exploration work and a feasibility study and did not plan to begin commercial production until late 1998.
Friedland criticized the coup leaders, calling them "mutineers," and said he doubted they would hold power for long. "This is a real slap against democracy...What they have done is wrong," he said.

But if they remain in power, DiamondWorks ultimately will have to negotiate with them to secure the future of its diamond properties. "...We would be forced to discuss with them. We are not just going to walk away from Sierra Leone," he said.
The Sierra Leone property represents about half the value of DiamondWorks' assets.

The company was more upbeat about its diamond properties in Angola and said it expects to begin commercial production of alluvial diamonds at its Luo project next week with the aim of producing 500 carats a day by the end of the year.
Friedland said stones from the site had an average value of US$400 a carat.
DiamondWorks is trying to convince Angola state diamond concern Endiama to allow it to sell diamonds in Antwerp where it believes it can fetch 10 to 25 percent higher prices.

Friedland said DiamondWorks expects to raise US$15 million to US$20 million in new financing by the end of the year and announced the appointment of Bruce Walsham as the company's new chief executive and president.
